name: Zane Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Whatever you tell me is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm foreman for a builder out in the country, about forty minutes from the nearest city. We do farm work mostly, machinery sheds, hay barns, cattle housing, and a few timber-frame houses for people moving out of town. Right now we're putting up a big steel-and-timber shed for a dairy farmer, so it's me, five men and a telehandler, that's a lifting machine with a long arm. I'm out of the house by half six, and I usually stop at the bakery where my wife Claire's sister works.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building for people I know. The farmer whose shed we're putting up, I went to school with his father. What's hard is the weather, and the travel between jobs, some days I'm two hours on the road. And getting young men to stick at it, they come for a summer and then they're off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A little, now and then. My son-in-law Ben showed me how to use one to write up quotes so they look professional, and it's good for that. I don't use it for anything that matters, like loads on a roof, I'd rather ask the engineer. But I'm not against it, if it saves me an hour at night, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, back to work. At church I'd say there's always some new thing people say will change the world. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I carry on as planned. Claire and I have savings, we own our five acres and a few head of cattle, so we're comfortable. I'd retire at sixty-three or so and spend more time with the animals and the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep using the AI for the quotes, keep running the crew. Maybe I'd push the boss to take on an apprentice, because we need young people coming through. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as any year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned getting young men to stick at it. Who would you take on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lad, Caleb, from the youth group at church, seventeen, good with his hands. I'd want him to learn properly, not just carry steel. In this picture I'd be pushing the boss to sign him up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything bother you about AI staying small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe I'd have liked it to help with the paperwork for the farm grants, that's a nightmare. But we've managed so far.

S0.say: That's that, back to work: there's always some new thing that's supposed to change the world. He'd say it at church, not online.
S0.think: He carries on as planned, comfortable with savings, five acres and a few cattle, and retires around sixty-three to spend time with animals and grandchildren.
S0.do: Keeps running the crew and using AI for quotes. Pushes the boss to take on a seventeen-year-old from the church youth group as an apprentice.
S0.quote: There's always some new thing people say will change the world.
S0.fieldNote: Zane's life is rooted in his rural community, building for families he's known for decades. His comfort comes from land and cattle as much as savings. His focus on apprenticeships for local young men shows his values about work and community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still going to be work for people who are willing to learn and work hard. At church I'd say the same. And I'd say businesses should be free to use what works, but they ought to train people too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not a lot changes. Out here the jobs are all different, a shed on a hill, a barn on a slope, so it's hard to automate. I'd use more of the AI for paperwork and quotes, and maybe for planning the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen a few other builders using it well, I'd get more serious about the planning and quoting tools, maybe a course at the farm college in the winter. I'd keep pushing for apprentices. And I'd tell my son, who's in sales in the city, to keep an eye on his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry for my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Luke, if a computer can do your job, it will. Sales is talking and writing, and these machines can do that. I'd tell him there's always work back here if he wants it, building or farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses should be free to use what works. What if it costs local jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the town has to look after its own. Families, churches, neighbours. I don't think the government is good at that, they'd send forms and money and nothing else.

S1.say: There'll still be work for people willing to learn and work hard. Businesses should be free to use what works, but they ought to train people too.
S1.think: Little changes for him, because rural jobs on hills and slopes are hard to automate. He'd use more AI for paperwork, quotes and planning.
S1.do: Gets more serious about planning and quoting tools once other builders use them well, perhaps with a winter course at the farm college. Keeps pushing for apprentices and warns his son in city sales to watch his job.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some worry for his son.
S1.quote: I'd say, Luke, if a computer can do your job, it will.
S1.fieldNote: Zane is calm about his own rural work and pushes worry onto his son's city sales job. He believes in businesses' freedom to adopt technology but expects them to train people. He trusts community over government to look after people who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll get through it, we always have. At church I'd say we need to look after each other and not panic. And I'd say businesses will do what they do, but families and communities have to stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be sixty, I'd probably stop. We've got the land and the savings, we'll be fine. But Luke's job in the city would be gone, and there'd be young men in town with nothing to do, and that worries me more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd talk to Claire about me stopping at sixty instead of sixty-three, before the boss has to decide for me. I'd tell Luke he can come home and help on the land, maybe we'd buy a few more cattle to make it worth his while. And I'd talk to the pastor about the church running something for young men out of work, a workshop or a building project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, we'll eat, but for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying more cattle sounds like a real expense. How much are you thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twenty more head, that's a good bit of money, and some fencing. But land and animals are real things, they don't vanish if a computer crashes. I'd rather put savings there than in a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the church project look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something real, like building a new hall or fixing up old houses for widows. Give the young men tools and something to do with their hands. Idle hands, you know the saying.

S2.say: We'll get through it, we always have. Businesses will do what they do, but families and communities have to stick together and look after each other without panicking.
S2.think: At sixty he'd probably stop, safe with land and savings. What worries him most is his son's city job vanishing and young men in town with nothing to do.
S2.do: Talks with his wife about stopping at sixty rather than sixty-three before the boss decides for him. Invites his son home to work the land, buying about twenty more cattle and fencing, and asks the pastor to start a church building project for young men out of work.
S2.feel: Uneasy for the young ones, not for himself.
S2.quote: Land and animals are real things, they don't vanish if a computer crashes.
S2.fieldNote: Even with fast AGI, Zane stays uneasy rather than anxious because his land and cattle feel solid. He'd put savings into livestock and bring his son home. His response to joblessness is a church building project, not government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people are sensible. At church I'd say prepare, help each other, keep working while you can. And I'd say the young ones should learn what the machines can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three, retired about when I planned. Luke would have time to move, and the town would have time to plan. I'm not too worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to sixty-three, use more of the AI tools as they prove themselves. I'd buy a few more cattle over the years, not all at once. And I'd talk to Luke about moving back in a few years, maybe building him a house on our land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. There's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Building a house for Luke, would you do that yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me and the crew, yes, on weekends. It'd be my last big job, a house for my own son. That would be a good way to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture you'd want to see done differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the big companies to keep apprenticeships going till the end, so young people learn something real. Even if the robots come, a young man who knows how to build is never helpless.

S3.say: Five years is enough if people are sensible: prepare, help each other, keep working while you can. Young people should learn what machines can't do.
S3.think: He'd retire at sixty-three as planned, his son and the town would have time to adjust, and he isn't too worried.
S3.do: Works to sixty-three and uses more AI tools as they prove themselves. Buys a few cattle over the years and plans to build his son a house on their land so he can move back.
S3.quote: It'd be my last big job, a house for my own son.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Zane plan calmly and turn his worry for his son into a family project. Building his son a house would be a fitting last job. He wants apprenticeships kept going because practical skill gives dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people have to use it well. At church I'd say the same, trust God and prepare. And I'd tell any young man to learn a trade and keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, with the cattle and the grandchildren. Luke and my daughter would have plenty of time to figure things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at sixty-three as planned and enjoy the land. I'd tell Luke to think about coming home, but no rush. And I'd wait and see what happens, because ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's too far away to worry about much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about building, in a world where robots do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Building for people I know. A robot doesn't know the farmer's father, doesn't know why he wants the shed facing east. That's what makes a building right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Caleb, the young lad from church, about 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn to build and to learn to fix the machines. Then he's covered whichever way it goes. And go to church, it keeps a man steady.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and people have to use it well: trust God and prepare. He'd tell any young man to learn a trade and keep learning.
S4.think: At sixty-eight he'd be retired with his cattle and grandchildren, and his children would have plenty of time to adjust.
S4.do: Retires at sixty-three as planned and enjoys the land. Invites his son to think about coming home without rushing him, and waits to see how things unfold.
S4.feel: Calm, because it's too far away to worry much.
S4.quote: A robot doesn't know the farmer's father, doesn't know why he wants the shed facing east.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Zane is calm and his concern is about what's lost in building for neighbours. His advice to young people is to cover both bases, building and fixing machines. Faith runs through his steadiness.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, for my son and the young men in town. What would help is businesses keeping apprenticeships going and helping people move into new work, and communities and churches being free to step in without the government getting in the way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to small towns. Out here, the builder, the mechanic, the baker, we all know each other. If the work goes to machines owned by companies in the city, the money leaves town and doesn't come back.

headlineQuote: If the work goes to machines owned by companies in the city, the money leaves town and doesn't come back.
portrait: Zane Dubois is a 58-year-old foreman for a country builder who puts up farm sheds, barns and timber-frame houses for people he's known all his life. He and his wife own five acres and some cattle, he's active in his church, and he uses AI now and then for quotes. He believes businesses should be free to use what works but should train people, and he trusts families and churches over government. Even fast AGI leaves him only uneasy, worried for his son's city sales job and the young men in town. With more time he plans calmly, invests in cattle and dreams of building his son a house as his last job.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, for his son and the young men in his town.
whatWouldHelp: Businesses keeping apprenticeships going and helping people move into new work, with communities and churches free to step in without government getting in the way.
